Capstone · Web design and development

AI Driving

For my capstone, I designed and coded a website for a fictional autonomous vehicle company. I wanted to apply my UX and web design skills to an industry I’d like to work in.

Design focus Make a technical subject easier to explore through clear navigation and page structure.

PROJECT CONTEXT

Project and approach

I got interested in automated vehicles by paying attention to how differently people make decisions on the road. I want to work on the part of vehicle automation people interact with. I’m curious about how we explain what the technology does, help people understand its limits, and make it easier to use in everyday life. For this project, I started with the website a person might visit to learn about the company and its services.

01 / DESIGN DECISIONS

Define what each page needs to do

I started with an HTML prototype so I could work through the navigation and decide where the calls to action and images belonged. Home introduces the company, About provides context, Services explains its offerings, and Contact gives interested visitors a clear next step.

02 / DESIGN DECISIONS

Refine the layout in the browser

I built the site in HTML and CSS and checked it on a laptop, desktop, and phone. Seeing it at different sizes helped me adjust how the navigation, text, and images fit together. I used a consistent blue and gray palette across the four pages.

03 / DESIGN DECISIONS

Explore the site and process report

My capstone report covers the early HTML prototype, device checks, and visual refinements. You can try the navigation and contact form on the demo site. The form is for demonstration only.

Open the demo website ↗Read the design-process report (PDF) ↗

REFLECTION

What I learned and what I’d test next

Building the site gave me practice turning an interest in vehicle automation into something people could explore. I’d test whether a first-time visitor can find a service and explain it in their own words. Longer term, I’d like to bring the same approach to onboarding and in-vehicle interfaces, where people need to know what an automated feature is doing and when it needs their attention.
